citation: Burkitt-type study, 'Children's colour use to portray themselves and others with happy, sad and mixed emotion', Educational Psychology 34(2), 2014, DOI 10.1080/01443410.2013.785059; contrasted with a separate study finding colour choice does not reliably reflect emotional content ('Does Children's Colour Use Reflect the Emotional Content of their Drawings?')
exact_measurable_visual_feature: Proportion/dominant category of warm vs. cool/dull colours used for a figure or scene
target_interpretation_or_construct: Represented emotional valence (happy/sad/mixed) of the depicted figure
population_ages_n_protocol: N=180 (90 girls, 90 boys), ages 4y11m-8y1m; INSTRUCTED task -- children told which emotion to portray
evidence_supporting: Children used colours differentially across drawing types; red/blue used differentially for mixed-emotion depictions; broader literature reports warm colours associated with positive feelings, dull/black/blue with negative
evidence_contradicting: A separate empirical study found children's colour choices do NOT reliably reflect emotional content -- colour PREFERENCE dominates regardless of emotional context. Direct contradiction, not a minor caveat.
effect_size_reliability_or_diagnostic_ac: Not precisely quantified from available abstracts/snippets; full-text retrieval would be needed for exact statistics. Treat as unquantified pending that retrieval.
alternative_explanations: Stable colour preference independent of emotion; available materials/palette; cultural convention; task demand characteristics from being told which emotion to draw
detector_measurement_requirements: NONE NEW -- DOAR's features.py already computes colour_proportions and dominant_colour
applicability_to_doar: Feature already measurable without new detector work, but underlying studies are INSTRUCTED-task, and the literature is directly self-contradictory on whether the relationship exists at all in any protocol
maximum_safe_interpretation: None justified as an operational rule given direct contradiction in the literature itself; at most, 'colour choice research is mixed and inconclusive' as a limitations note
verification_status: Web search summaries only; exact statistics not retrieved from full text this session

citation: LaRoque & Obrzut, 'Pencil Pressure and Anxiety in Drawings: A Techno-Projective Approach', Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment, 2006, DOI/URL: journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0734282906288520
exact_measurable_visual_feature: Physical pencil/stylus pressure (force) applied during drawing, measured via a pressure-sensitive digitizing tablet at capture time
population_ages_n_protocol: Ages 6-11; pressure-sensitive palette; INSTRUCTED tasks: Draw-A-Person, Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test, drawing an automobile. Exact N not confirmed from available summary.
evidence_supporting: Higher trait anxiety -> significantly LESS pencil pressure across all 3 tasks. State anxiety showed a curvilinear relationship: both high AND low state anxiety produced MORE pressure than medium state anxiety -- a non-monotonic finding, not a simple linear one.
evidence_contradicting: General literature on drawing-based assessment techniques (not this study specifically) raises 'substantial doubts about reliability and validity'; lack of standardized empirical scoring methods across the field
effect_size_reliability_or_diagnostic_ac: Not precisely quantified from available summary; full-text retrieval needed
alternative_explanations: Drawing instrument/paper/tablet texture; fine-motor development (strongly age-correlated); fatigue; task engagement/effort
detector_measurement_requirements: The VALIDATED measurement (physical pressure via digitizer) is NOT recoverable from a static scanned/photographed image after the fact -- DOAR only ever receives a final flattened image, never capture-time pressure data. Only an indirect, unvalidated proxy (ink/graphite darkness, stroke-width variability) is available from static images.
applicability_to_doar: LOW -- the specific validated construct (digitizer pressure) is structurally unmeasurable from DOAR's input format. DOAR's existing stroke.intensity_proxy is NOT the same construct as this literature validates and must not be presented as if it were.
maximum_safe_interpretation: None currently justified; if ever explored, must be labeled explicitly as an unvalidated proxy for a different, unmeasurable construct
verification_status: Web search summary only; exact N and effect sizes not retrieved from full text this session

citation: Koppitz emotional-indicator system for Human Figure Drawings (widely studied; summarized via multiple secondary sources this session, primary Koppitz text not directly retrieved)
exact_measurable_visual_feature: Composite count of ~30 discrete HFD signs: omissions (body parts), distortions, size anomalies, shading, asymmetry, etc.
target_interpretation_or_construct: General emotional/behavioural disturbance, grouped into impulsivity, insecurity, anxiety, shyness, aggression categories
population_ages_n_protocol: Multiple studies, general child/adolescent clinical and community samples; INSTRUCTED (Draw-A-Person)
evidence_supporting: Severely disturbed children's drawings showed HIGHER indicator counts than matched controls -- a real, replicated finding at the severe end of the distribution
evidence_contradicting: The same indicators 'failed to differentiate between clinical and normally-adjusted children's drawings on AVERAGE scores' -- i.e. does not work as a general clinical-vs-typical discriminator, only shows signal for severe cases
effect_size_reliability_or_diagnostic_ac: Goodenough-Harris DEVELOPMENTAL/cognitive-maturity scoring (a different construct) reports reliability >=.90; this does not transfer to the emotional-indicator system's validity, which remains disputed per the sources above
alternative_explanations: Developmental/fine-motor immaturity produces many of the same 'indicators' (omissions, distortions) independent of emotional state -- a well-documented confound in this literature
detector_measurement_requirements: A full human-figure part-presence/distortion detector -- substantially beyond anything in DOAR's current Phase 3 scope (would need per-body-part keypoint/presence detection, size-anomaly measurement relative to a body-proportion norm, shading measurement per region)
applicability_to_doar: Theoretically Tier-2-adjacent (content-conditional on a person being drawn) but far beyond current detector roadmap; no existing DOAR rule attempts this composite-count structure
maximum_safe_interpretation: At most: 'an unusually high count of these signs together may relate to severe disturbance in instructed DAP contexts; not established for typical variation, not established for spontaneous drawing, confounded by motor/developmental factors'
verification_status: Secondary-source summaries only; primary Koppitz texts and the specific studies behind these claims were not directly retrieved this session

citation: 'The Application of Human Figure Drawing as a Supplementary Tool for Depression Screening', PMC9204051 -- fetched and read directly this session
exact_measurable_visual_feature: Figure size; omitted hands/eyes/nose/feet/eyebrows; shaded hair/eyebrows/nose/mouth/eyes; detail level of clothes/accessories/limbs/facial features/personal belongings (17 features total)
population_ages_n_protocol: Clinical N=113, mean age 31.04 (SD 17.57), 70.8% female, clinically diagnosed MDD; Control N=97, mean age 18.46 (SD 0.87), 70.1% male, college students SDS<50. INSTRUCTED: 'draw a complete person with a pencil on A4 paper', no time limit.
evidence_supporting: Small size: chi2=10.060, p=.002, r=.159 with SDS score (weak). Hands omitted: chi2=6.605, p=.010. Detailed clothes: chi2=16.723, p<.001, OR=6.849, r=-.183 (more detail associated with LOWER depression). Personal belongings: chi2=28.854, p<.001, OR=6.274, r=-.219. Shaded eyes: OR=0.278, p=.034 in logistic regression (protective direction, i.e. opposite of the naive 'shading=distress' folk claim).
evidence_contradicting: Shaded eyes was significant by logistic regression (p=.034) but NOT significant by ROC/AUC analysis (AUC=0.543, p=.285) -- internally inconsistent across statistical methods for the SAME feature, a fragility flag. Eyes/nose omission, left-sided placement, shaded mouth, and accessory detail were all non-significant. Best AUCs (detailed clothes 0.627, personal belongings 0.637) are only modestly above chance (0.5).
effect_size_reliability_or_diagnostic_ac: Nagelkerke R^2=0.641 for the full logistic model (not per-feature); best single-feature AUCs 0.62-0.64; authors explicitly state 'sensitivity of HFD is relatively low' and recommend the test be 'considered as a whole instead of focusing on' single features
alternative_explanations: Authors note small sample size and no test-retest reliability assessment (cross-sectional design); age/gender were controlled for in regression but the two groups still differ hugely in mean age (31 vs 18.5) raising residual confounding concern
detector_measurement_requirements: Figure-size measurement (plausibly reuse existing bbox-coverage-style features); hand-omission detection (needs body-part/keypoint detector, not yet built); eye-shading measurement (needs face/eye localization + local shading intensity, not yet built)
applicability_to_doar: BLOCKED on two independent grounds: (1) population is ADULTS (mean ages 31 and 18.5), not children -- DOAR analyses children's drawings; (2) protocol is INSTRUCTED Draw-A-Person, not spontaneous free drawing. Neither the construct (adult MDD) nor the protocol match DOAR's scope.
maximum_safe_interpretation: None for DOAR directly. Useful only as general context: even in a well-controlled, well-reported instructed-adult study, single HFD features show modest and sometimes internally-inconsistent associations -- reinforcing why DOAR's existing confidence ceilings (0.05-0.25) are appropriately conservative.
verification_status: VERIFIED -- full text read directly via PMC this session, statistics quoted from the source

citation: Davis-Kean & Sandler, 'A Meta-Analysis of Measures of Self-Esteem for Young Children: A Framework for Future Measures', PubMed 11405589
exact_measurable_visual_feature: N/A -- this is a meta-analysis of ASSESSMENT METHODS (questionnaire vs. drawing-based vs. other), not a specific visual feature
target_interpretation_or_construct: Self-esteem measurement reliability, compared across method types
population_ages_n_protocol: Meta-analysis aggregating multiple young-children self-esteem studies; not a single primary sample
evidence_supporting: Questionnaire-based self-esteem measures were found MORE reliable than measures using drawings or other tools as aids -- a direct, general caution against drawing-based self-esteem inference from a meta-analytic source
evidence_contradicting: None found contradicting this specific meta-analytic conclusion in this search pass
effect_size_reliability_or_diagnostic_ac: Reliability found to be predicted by study setting, scale item count, child age, data-collection method, and SES -- drawing-based collection was one method among several found less reliable, exact reliability coefficients not retrieved from full text this session
alternative_explanations: N/A -- this is itself a methodological finding, not a claim requiring alternative explanation
detector_measurement_requirements: None -- this is a citation to strengthen an existing rule's documented limitations, not a new detector target
applicability_to_doar: Directly reinforces the EXISTING rule PSY_AR_SIZE_FULL_015 (coverage_full -> 'high self-esteem'), which is already flagged not_found_for_threshold_claim. This meta-analysis is additional, general supporting evidence for that existing scepticism, not a new rule.
maximum_safe_interpretation: Strengthens the case that PSY_AR_SIZE_FULL_015's confidence ceiling (0.15) should stay low or be reconsidered downward, never raised
recommendation: RESEARCH-ONLY (reinforcing citation for an existing rule, not a new operational candidate)
verification_status: Web search summary only; exact reliability coefficients not retrieved from full text this session

citation: 'Quantifying developmental and individual differences in spontaneous drawing completion among children', PMC9697182 -- fetched and read directly this session
exact_measurable_visual_feature: Proportion of representational vs. scribble content; CNN-extracted hierarchical visual features measuring adaptation to a partial stimulus
target_interpretation_or_construct: NONE PSYCHOLOGICAL -- purely developmental/maturational drawing-skill stage. Explicitly NOT proposed as an emotional or diagnostic indicator.
population_ages_n_protocol: N=104 children (62M/42F), 621 drawings, ages 2y1m-8y3m; plus 107 drawings from 5 adults for comparison. NOT free drawing -- a structured 'drawing completion' paradigm: children complete a partially-drawn stimulus (outline-only / inner-features-shown / scrambled-inner-features), across 4 object categories (face, house, car, human figure).
spontaneous_or_instructed: NEITHER purely spontaneous nor verbally instructed -- a stimulus-completion paradigm distinct from both DOAR's free-drawing definition and standard instructed prompts. The paper's own title uses 'spontaneous' loosely; this must not be read as validating DOAR's specific free-drawing (no stimulus at all) context.
evidence_supporting: With increasing age, children exhibit more representational drawings and less scribbling (p<.001) -- a robust, expected, unconflicted developmental finding. Older children adapted their drawings more similarly to adults than younger children did.
evidence_contradicting: No correlation between drawing behaviour and autistic traits (AQ scores) was found in this sample -- a null result reported honestly by the authors, not evidence against the age-finding itself
effect_size_reliability_or_diagnostic_ac: p<.001 for the age/representational-content relationship; authors note relatively small sample despite exceeding prior studies, and low AQ-score variability limiting the null-result's power
alternative_explanations: Fine-motor development, task familiarity/practice, and general cognitive maturation all plausibly co-vary with age alongside representational drawing ability
detector_measurement_requirements: A scribble-vs-representational classifier is plausibly buildable from DOAR's EXISTING connected-component/stroke/fragmentation features (features.py) with no new external detector or dataset -- lowest-dependency candidate in this entire register
applicability_to_doar: HIGH as an OBJECTIVE, non-psychological descriptive feature. DOAR does not currently collect or use age, but this feature could be computed and reported purely descriptively without needing age at all (e.g. 'this drawing shows more scribble-like / more representational characteristics'), and could plausibly serve as a covariate to help interpret or improve the emotion classifier (a scribbly drawing from a very young child looks visually very different from an intentional 'Sad' drawing from an older child, independent of actual felt emotion) -- directly the kind of 'objective observation that improves model performance even when no psychological interpretation is justified' requested.
maximum_safe_interpretation: Purely descriptive only -- 'this drawing shows characteristics more typical of [scribble/representational] stage.' NEVER an emotional, personality, or diagnostic claim, and never used to infer the child's actual age (drawing skill varies for many reasons besides age).
recommendation: OPERATIONAL CANDIDATE (as an objective Tier-1 descriptive feature / potential model covariate ONLY -- explicitly NOT as a psychological rule)
verification_status: VERIFIED -- full text read directly via PMC this session, statistics quoted from the source
